new_statements.quote: El acento puinave, que representamos con el símbolo /ˊ/ es un acento de carácter melódico. El elemento de fuerza existe pero es secundario. La sílaba que lleva el acento se pronuncia en un tono musical más alto que las demás sílabas de la unidad a la cual pertenece. Esta estructura musical del acento puinave permite la presencia de varios de ellos en la misma unidad lingüística, cosa que nunca ocurre con un acento de fuerza. [...] No se trata, sin embargo, de un tono propiamente dicho, como p. ej., en chino, sino de un acento melódico del tipo sueco o japonés [...] Es, pues, un acento típicamente diferenciativo y por esta razón lo consideramos como un fonema separado.
new_statements.translation: The Puinave accent, which we represent with the symbol /ˊ/, is an accent of melodic character. The force (intensity) element exists but is secondary. The syllable bearing the accent is pronounced at a higher musical pitch than the other syllables of the unit to which it belongs. This musical structure of the Puinave accent allows several of them to be present in the same linguistic unit, something that never happens with a stress accent. [...] It is not, however, a tone properly speaking, as e.g. in Chinese, but a melodic accent of the Swedish or Japanese type [...] It is thus a typically distinctive accent and for this reason we treat it as a separate phoneme.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Wãnsöjöt has an empty rule; Caudmont supplies the type (lexically distinctive pitch accent, a phoneme, no positional rule) and the phonetic cue (pitch, with intensity secondary). Girón 2008 (p. 14) cites this as Caudmont's 34-phoneme system 'incluyendo 1 acento'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence is a pitch (melodic) accent, marked /ˊ/, realised as a higher musical pitch on the accented syllable; intensity is secondary. It is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs, especially monosyllables, e.g. /wãn/ 'toucan' vs /wan/ 'fox', fn. 7) and is counted as one of the 34 phonemes. More than one accent may occur in the same unit. No positional rule (initial/penult/etc.) is given; placement is lexical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None as such; the author says the force element 'exists but is secondary' and that several melodic accents may occur in one unit.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author explicitly denies that this is Chinese-style tone and compares it to Swedish/Japanese pitch accent 'at least in its acoustic structure', distributing vowels over two levels, low and high.
new_statements.identity_note: Caudmont 1954 is based on a short recorded survey with Puinave rubber tappers ('indios caucheros'), principal informant 'el indio Pedro', in 1950s Colombia (p. 267). Girón 2008 describes the Wãnsöjöt of the Inírida river region (Puerto Inírida, Alto Inírida and Yurí communities), Guainía, Colombia. Both are the same language (Glottolog puin1248); no separate dialects are distinguished by either source.

new_statements.quote: El sistema de prosodia de la palabra en wãnsöjöt tiene la restricción de asociar como máximo un tono H por morfema (una sola sílaba H). De allí que dicho tono funcione como una prominencia acentual, lo que no obvia que también existan palabras sin ninguna prominencia acentual (aquellas donde no hay ningún tono H). [p. 109] Sólo puede haber como máximo un tono H por morfema, el cual está asociado a una sola vocal. En morfemas polisílabos no es previsible el lugar de asociación de dicho tono H. [p. 110] En síntesis, en wãnsöjöt la prominencia prosódica está dada por una sílaba con tono H o HL. [p. 142]
new_statements.translation: The word-prosody system of Wãnsöjöt has the restriction of associating at most one H tone per morpheme (a single H syllable). Hence that tone functions as an accentual prominence, which does not preclude the existence of words with no accentual prominence at all (those with no H tone). [p. 109] There can be at most one H tone per morpheme, associated with a single vowel. In polysyllabic morphemes the place of association of that H tone is not predictable. [p. 110] In sum, in Wãnsöjöt prosodic prominence is carried by a syllable with H or HL tone. [p. 142]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule is empty; Girón supplies a full analysis: tonal (four melodies), with a culminative H/HL 'accentual' prominence whose position is lexically unpredictable, and no intensity-based stress. Relative to Caudmont 1954 it agrees on the essentials (pitch is the cue, intensity secondary, lexically distinctive, multiple pitch peaks possible) but classifies the system as tone with contour tones rather than a single accent phoneme.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wãnsöjöt is analysed as a tone language: four contrastive melodies on monosyllables (H, L, HL, LH; §6.1, p. 104-105), tone is part of lexical representation for nouns, verbs, adverbs and pronouns, while bound pronouns, particles and affixes are toneless and get default tone. Word-level prominence is not stress: intensity by itself does not mark prosodic prominence (p. 107). Instead the system is 'tono-acentual': at most one H (or HL) per morpheme, which is the culminative prominence; its position in bi- and trisyllabic morphemes is lexically unpredictable (initial, final or medial, ex. 223 p. 111), and words with no H have no prominence. Pitch is the primary cue; duration and intensity are predictable from tone (p. 106). Girón adds (p. 137) that since H and HL do not spread, 'podría suponerse que la función de estos tonos es básicamente acentual'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None. In polysyllables with L tone no syllable can be unambiguously identified as more accented, though the final tends to be more intense (fn. 137, p. 111); utterance-initial syllables tend to be higher and more energetic than final ones (p. 107), a phrase-level effect.
new_statements.exceptions: Contour tones do not occur on word-final open CV syllables; HL splits into H-L under agentive derivation and sporadically in verbal derivation, PL inflection and compounding; LH occurs only in monosyllables and a few disyllables, never in trisyllabic morphemes; no correlation between syllable weight and tone (p. 108); tonal changes under derivation are 'de gran irregularidad' (§6.8, p. 137).
new_statements.identity_note: Caudmont 1954 is based on a short recorded survey with Puinave rubber tappers ('indios caucheros'), principal informant 'el indio Pedro', in 1950s Colombia (p. 267). Girón 2008 describes the Wãnsöjöt of the Inírida river region (Puerto Inírida, Alto Inírida and Yurí communities), Guainía, Colombia. Both are the same language (Glottolog puin1248); no separate dialects are distinguished by either source.

readall_conflicts: The two sources agree on the substance and differ on the label. Caudmont 1954 (p. 274) calls the prominence a 'melodic accent' of the Swedish/Japanese type, a distinctive phoneme realised as higher pitch with intensity secondary, explicitly 'not a tone properly speaking, as in Chinese'; several accents may occur in one unit; no positional rule is given. Girón 2008 (pp. 104-111, 142) analyses the same facts as a tone system with four contrastive melodies (H, L, HL, LH) on monosyllables, contour tones, spreading and OCP effects, and then states that the single H (or HL) per morpheme functions as a culminative 'accentual' prominence whose position in polysyllables is lexically unpredictable, while intensity alone does not mark prominence (p. 107). So Caudmont = pitch accent, Girón = tone with an accent-like culminative H; both deny an intensity-based word stress and both give no positional rule. Girón himself concedes (p. 137) that the function of the non-spreading H and HL tones 'is basically accentual', so the disagreement is one of analytic framing, not of data.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (tone-accent: contrastive H/L/HL/LH melodies, culminative max-one-H per morpheme, lexically unpredictable H position, intensity not a word-prominence cue) rests on the language's only reference grammar (Girón 2008, LOT 185, 476 pp), held as PDF+text, and every fragment of the deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim at the stated pages (104, 107, 109-110). The source is modern, by the principal fieldworker, includes instrumental F0/intensity observations, and its analysis is independently echoed in Hyman 2009 and Hyman 2010 (held elsewhere in our check tree) via Girón Higuita & Wetzels 2007. The only newer work is a 2023 handbook sketch co-authored by Girón (paywalled), which could at most refine terminology. no reclassification or re-read is indicated.
